outcome: No accepted resolution or counterexample has appeared since 26 January 2024 in any source I could open. Two single-author arXiv papers claim the full statement (Pasku, first posted 2021, revised 5 Oct 2026; Kawauchi, first posted 2023, revised Apr 2024) and neither shows public review; the two most recent papers by Roman Mikhailov (Aug and Oct 2026) call the question open and cite neither. The only new AI-credited mathematics bearing on the bullet (Bartholdi and Mikhailov, 7 Oct 2026) gives finite chains only, and an OpenAI counterexample to the Eilenberg-Ganea conjecture (released 6 Oct 2026) has no stated bearing on Whitehead's conjecture.
problem_asks: (a) For every two-dimensional aspherical CW complex K and every connected subcomplex L of K: L is aspherical (all higher homotopy groups of L vanish). The bullet is universal over K and L; it names no finiteness, group class, or dimension restriction beyond 'two-dimensional' for K, so infinite complexes and infinite subcomplexes are included. (b) Not in the bullet, but stated in the literature as equivalent: every subpresentation of an aspherical group presentation (obtained by dropping some relators) is aspherical. The bullet does not ask for a counterexample, a bound, or a restricted case; a case settles part of it only if it covers some K and L.

events.what_happened: Mladen Bestvina and Noel Brady, 'Morse theory and finiteness properties of groups', Invent. Math. 129 (1997) 445-470. They construct a group G (reported as finitely presented) such that either G is a counterexample to the Eilenberg-Ganea conjecture or the Whitehead conjecture has a counterexample. The dichotomy is quoted by the Wikipedia pages for both conjectures and by later papers. I did not open the Inventiones article.
events.delivers: A constraint, not a resolution: the Whitehead and Eilenberg-Ganea conjectures cannot both be true. Whitehead true would force Eilenberg-Ganea false; Eilenberg-Ganea true would force Whitehead false. It does not say which, if either, fails.
events.remains: Both conjectures, as far as this result goes.
events.direction: Neither; it constrains the pair of conjectures.

events.what_happened: J. Howie, 'Some remarks on a problem of J. H. C. Whitehead', Topology 22 (1983) 475-485. Per later papers that cite it (Bartholdi-Mikhailov 2026, Harlander-Rosebrock, Cerdeiro-Minian), Howie showed that a counterexample must take one of two forms: (a) a finite contractible 2-complex L with K = L minus one 2-cell not aspherical, or (b) L the union of an infinite ascending chain of finite non-aspherical subcomplexes. Several later papers also attribute to Howie that a finite counterexample yields one among labelled oriented trees, up to the Andrews-Curtis conjecture. The Topology article itself was not opened; these statements come from the secondary sources.
events.delivers: A reduction of the search space: any counterexample is of form (a) or (b). It shows no subcomplex to be aspherical or non-aspherical.
events.remains: The whole bullet: no counterexample of either form is exhibited, and no subcomplex is shown aspherical.
events.direction: Neutral: a description of what a counterexample could look like.

events.what_happened: S. V. Ivanov, 'Some remarks on the Whitehead asphericity conjecture', Illinois J. Math. 43(4) (1999) 793-799. The abstract, as read: if the Whitehead conjecture is false there is an aspherical presentation of the trivial group, with alphabet finite or countably infinite, whose subpresentation <A||R> is not aspherical; and if it fails for finite presentations, there is a finite aspherical presentation with a non-aspherical subpresentation. A search summary attributes to the body a sharpening to the single-relator case (a relator that is a generator z); I did not verify this, since the full text is paywalled.
events.delivers: A reduction: a counterexample to the Whitehead conjecture, if one exists, can be taken to be an aspherical presentation of the trivial group, with a relator z whose deletion destroys asphericity. Finite presentation case as stated in the abstract. This is not a resolution.

checked_by.who: Illinois Journal of Mathematics (journal of record)

events.doubts: The single-relator refinement is from a search summary and is not verified. The abstract's notation for the finite case is partly garbled in the fetched text.
events.direction: Reduction; neutral on truth.

events.what_happened: Jens Harlander and Stephan Rosebrock, 'Injective labelled oriented trees are aspherical', arXiv:1212.1943 (December 2012); later published in Math. Z. (2017), per a search summary. Shows that injective labelled oriented tree (LOT) complexes, which are spines of ribbon disk-link complements, are aspherical. Not opened by me; the statement is from search summaries and from the 2025 paper's background section.
events.revisions: Journal version Math. Z. (2017) per search summary; not verified.
events.delivers: Asphericity of one restricted class: injective LOT complexes. LOT complexes are the class to which Howie's reduction directs any counterexample search, so this is partial progress within the reduced class, not a resolution.
events.remains: Non-injective LOT complexes, and all other 2-complexes; the full bullet.
events.doubts: Journal publication per search summary only. I did not read the arXiv text.
events.direction: Partial, toward the conjecture, within the reduced LOT class.

events.what_happened: Elton Pasku, 'A semigroup theoretic approach to Whitehead's asphericity question', arXiv:1407.6283, first posted 23 Jul 2014 with seven versions to 22 Jan 2019. The abstract, as read: it introduces a 'weak dominion' of a submonoid and gives a necessary and sufficient combinatorial condition for a subpresentation of an aspherical presentation to be aspherical. A search summary describes an earlier version titled 'A proof for the Whitehead asphericity problem'; I could not confirm that title or any claim of proof. Versions 2 and 4 are marked withdrawn.
events.revisions: v1 23 Jul 2014; v2 31 Jul 2014 (withdrawn); v3 4 Aug 2014; v4 6 Aug 2014 (withdrawn); v5 22 Sep 2014; v6 9 Apr 2016; v7 22 Jan 2019.
events.delivers: A reformulation: a necessary and sufficient condition, in semigroup terms, for subpresentation asphericity (per the abstract as read). On the abstract, no resolution of the question is claimed.
events.remains: The question, unless the body contains a proof (not established by me).
events.doubts: Withdrawn versions; a title change reported by a search summary; the 2021 Pasku paper acknowledges text overlap with this one. Whether an earlier version claimed a proof is unresolved in my reading.

withdrawn.what: arXiv:1407.6283 versions 2 and 4 are marked '(withdrawn)'. The page carries no notice text.

events.direction: Neutral: a characterisation of the subpresentation condition.

events.what_happened: Manuela Ana Cerdeiro and Elias Gabriel Minian, 'A new approach to Whitehead's asphericity question', arXiv:1203.5348 (23 Mar 2012), published in J. Homotopy Relat. Struct. (2013). The abstract, as read, restates the question using the homotopy theory of finite topological spaces and introduces a reduction method. Search summaries say they show certain classes of finite spaces, and hence compact complexes, satisfy their restated Conjecture 3.1; I did not read the body to check the restated form or the classes.
events.delivers: Partial, in a restated form: per search summaries, finite-space classes (and so compact complexes) that satisfy the restated conjecture. The abstract claims no resolution of the original question. Exact classes and whether the restated form is equivalent to the original were not verified.
events.remains: The original question for the general case.

checked_by.who: Journal of Homotopy and Related Structures (journal of record)
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the article (2013), per the Springer record found in search.

events.doubts: Body not read; the class restrictions come from search summaries.
events.direction: Neutral reformulation with partial class results toward the conjecture (unverified in the body).

events.what_happened: A. M. Mikhovich, 'Rational and p-adic analogs of J.H.C. Whitehead's conjecture', arXiv:2105.00281 (v1 1 May 2021; v2 16 Sep 2021). Published in Izvestiya: Mathematics 89:2 (2025), DOI 10.4213/im9597 (journal reference from the arXiv page; the mathnet record was unreachable). Abstract as read: subpresentations of aspherical prounipotent presentations over fields of characteristic zero, and of aspherical pro-p presentations, are aspherical; an application to aspherical discrete presentations is also included. The author calls these affirmative answers to the rational and p-adic analogues, not to the original.
events.revisions: v1 1 May 2021; v2 16 Sep 2021 (minor corrections; Section 6 on applications added). Journal: Izvestiya Mathematics 89:2 (2025).
events.delivers: Affirmative answers to the rational (characteristic zero, prounipotent) and p-adic (pro-p) analogues. These are analogues, not the bullet. The abstract also mentions an application to discrete presentations, whose strength I did not establish.
events.remains: The original discrete statement as the bullet words it.
events.doubts: A search summary reports the 2025 paper describes the classical question as still open. I did not read the body to confirm this.
events.direction: Analogue only; neutral on the bullet.

events.what_happened: Elton Pasku, 'An answer to the Whitehead asphericity question', arXiv:2107.12293 (v1 26 Jul 2021; v2 5 Oct 2026). Claims: if P = (x, r) is an aspherical presentation of the trivial group and r0 is a fixed relator, then P1 = (x, r minus {r0}) is aspherical. Using Ivanov's 1999 reduction, the paper says this gives a positive answer to the Whitehead question; combined with Bestvina-Brady it says the Eilenberg-Ganea conjecture is false. Method as outlined in the fetched text: Brown-Huebschmann identity-sequence criterion; a monoid and weak-dominion reformulation (Section 3); a topological approach via an extended Squier complex with a short exact sequence (Section 4), citing Pride and Otto-Kobayashi. The fetch covered about the first 100k of 148k characters.
events.revisions: v1 26 Jul 2021 (32 KB). v2 5 Oct 2026 (51 KB; 41 pages; comment 'arXiv admin note: text overlap with arXiv:1407.6283'). I did not identify what v2 changed.
events.delivers: If correct: the Whitehead question has a positive answer for every aspherical presentation of the trivial group (no finiteness is stated in the abstract). By Ivanov's reduction this excludes every candidate counterexample, so it covers the whole statement. The paper also claims the Eilenberg-Ganea conjecture is false.
events.remains: Nothing, on the paper's own claim. I did not check the proof.
events.time_since_posted: 5 years 2 months (v1 to 10 Oct 2026); v2 posted 5 days before that date
events.doubts: (1) No referee report, journal record, citation by a topologist, or published comment was found in any source I searched; arXiv's references page for the paper shows no citing papers. (2) The Aug 2026 and Oct 2026 papers by Roman Mikhailov (the second with Laurent Bartholdi) call the question open and neither cites Pasku or Kawauchi; Mikhailov is co-author of only the second. (3) The author's earlier arXiv:1407.6283 has withdrawn versions. (4) A small-model fetch summary quotes the paper as saying one equivalence 'might be as hard as the study of Peiffer operations' and that 'at this point it seems we have not made any progress at all', adding that the definition becomes useful later. I could not verify this wording in the PDF. (5) ProofAtlas's individual page (checked 7 Aug 2026) lists it as an unreviewed claim, not a solution.
events.direction: Toward the conjecture: claims it true for every aspherical presentation of the trivial group, hence the statement.

events.what_happened: Akio Kawauchi, 'Ribbonness of Kervaire's sphere-link in homotopy 4-sphere and its consequences to 2-complexes', arXiv:2212.02617 (December 2022; v3 exists). Per a search summary of the abstract: a ribbon disk-link presentation of every contractible finite 2-complex makes the exterior of each such link aspherical, so every connected subcomplex of a contractible finite 2-complex is aspherical. The author calls this a partial result toward Whitehead's conjecture. Not opened by me.
events.revisions: v3 exists (revised explanations, per search summary); dates of v2 and v3 not established.
events.delivers: Restricted to subcomplexes of contractible finite 2-complexes. It does not cover infinite complexes or aspherical complexes that are not contractible.
events.remains: Aspherical 2-complexes that are not contractible, infinite complexes, and the full bullet.
events.doubts: The author's own abstract calls the result 'partially yes'. Howie's finite contractible counterexamples of form (a) lie in this class, so the result rules out form (a) only; a search summary attributes to Luft (1996, one source, not verified) that form (a) implies form (b), so this alone does not close the question.
events.direction: Partial, toward the conjecture, on a restricted class.

events.what_happened: Akio Kawauchi, 'Whitehead aspherical conjecture via ribbon sphere-link', arXiv:2303.04368 (v1 8 Mar 2023; v2 9 Apr 2024). Claims 'Whitehead Aspherical Conjecture is true' (Theorem 1.1): every connected subcomplex of every aspherical 2-complex is aspherical. Structure per the v2 HTML, read through a fetch summary and not checked line by line: Conjecture 3 (homology-trivial unit-group presentations) implies Conjecture 2 (contractible locally finite 2-complexes), which implies Conjecture 1 (the statement), via Lemmas 2.1-2.3 and 3.2 with Cor 3.3. Conjecture 3 is proved using a ribbon S-squared link in R^4 (Lemma 4.1), asphericity of the exterior of a ribbon disk-link in H^4 (Lemma 5.1), and identification of 1-full subcomplexes with exteriors of sublinks (Thm 5.2, Cor 5.3). Lemma 4.1 relies on a 'Free Ribbon Lemma' from an earlier preprint. The paper mentions a preprint by E. Pasku reporting the same result by a purely group-theoretic argument, and calls its own argument 'much different'.
events.revisions: v1 8 Mar 2023: abstract says the earlier contractible finite case is generalised to every aspherical 2-complex. v2 9 Apr 2024: abstract in substance the same; the specific change is not identified. OCAMI preprint 24-5 (11 Apr 2024). The author's own publications list gives 'J. Math. Techniques Comput. Math. 3(5) (2024), 01-10'; this is self-reported and I could not find the journal record.
events.delivers: Claims the full statement: every connected subcomplex of every aspherical 2-complex is aspherical. No restriction is claimed. The argument as read goes through homology-trivial unit-group presentations, then contractible locally finite complexes, then the general case.
events.remains: Nothing, if the argument is correct.
events.time_since_posted: 3 years 7 months (v1 to 10 Oct 2026); 2 years 6 months since v2
events.doubts: (1) No referee report, correction, or citation by a topologist was found. Mikhailov's Aug 2026 paper and the Oct 2026 Bartholdi-Mikhailov paper call the question open and cite neither Kawauchi nor Pasku. (2) Fetch-summary notes, not checked against the PDF: Lemma 3.1 uses an 'informal Euclidean-type reduction' whose termination for infinite bases is not clear; Lemma 3.2 refers forward to a base-change matrix 'given in Lemma 3.3'; the H^4_+ and H^4_- definitions in Lemma 5.1 appear inconsistent; Lemma 4.1 depends on a 'Free Ribbon Lemma' from an earlier preprint cited only by a website link. (3) The author's website lists a 2024 journal publication that I could not verify, so I have not counted it as a check. (4) The author's website flags incomplete proofs and errors in other papers (boundary and stable-ribbon surface-links), not in this one.
events.direction: Toward the conjecture: claims it true for every aspherical 2-complex.

events.what_happened: Akio Kawauchi, 'Free ribbon lemma for surface-link', arXiv:2412.09281 (v1 12 Dec 2024; six versions to 4 Oct 2025). The abstract states that every free sphere-link in S^4 is ribbon (the Free Ribbon Lemma) and refers to 'an earlier paper' containing a first proof. It does not mention Whitehead's question.
events.delivers: A lemma on surface-links: free sphere-links are ribbon. Nothing about the bullet.
events.doubts: Its bearing on the 2023 argument is unestablished: the abstract does not say which earlier paper is meant, and I did not confirm that this is the lemma Lemma 4.1 relies on.
events.direction: Neutral for the bullet.

events.what_happened: Jens Harlander and Stephan Rosebrock, 'Local indicability in the presence of diagrammatic reducibility', arXiv:2511.15212 (v1 19 Nov 2025; v2 31 May 2026). The arXiv page lists DOI 10.4153/S0008439526102069, probably a Canadian Mathematical Bulletin record that I did not confirm. Abstract as read: if X is a subcomplex of a diagrammatically reducible (DR) 2-complex Y whose fundamental group is locally indicable, then X is DR and has locally indicable fundamental group; an injective labelled oriented tree (LOT) that is DR of degree 2, along with all its quotients, is locally indicable. The abstract says these bear on Whitehead's asphericity conjecture.
events.revisions: v1 19 Nov 2025; v2 31 May 2026 (changes not identified).
events.delivers: Restricted: local indicability and DR for subcomplexes of DR complexes, and for injective LOT complexes of degree 2 with all their quotients. It does not address general 2-complexes. It is a step inside the LOT class that Howie's reduction points to.
events.remains: The general statement, and every 2-complex outside the LOT and DR-degree-2 hypotheses.
events.direction: Restricted toward the conjecture (LOT class); neutral for the general statement.

events.what_happened: Roman Mikhailov, 'Two results on asphericity', arXiv:2608.20270 (submitted 20 Aug 2026; one version). Abstract as read: constructs an explicit finite chain of non-aspherical group presentation complexes, built from a short balanced presentation of the binary icosahedral group, answering a question of Hitchman; and an integral Lie ring presentation whose subpresentation has a nontrivial identity among relations. The paper states that Whitehead's asphericity question 'remains open'. Per a search summary, the chain has length two, with zero maps on second homotopy groups.
events.delivers: A finite chain of length two of non-aspherical presentation complexes, with zero second-homotopy inclusion maps (per search summary). It answers Hitchman's question. It does not address the Whitehead question except to state that it is open. Its chain is finite and so is not the infinite chain that a negative answer would need.
events.doubts: AI use statement (not recorded in ai.systems, because the authors describe writing assistance): 'This text was written with the assistance of ChatGPT 5.6 Sol.' and 'Working with AI was an iterative process, making it difficult to isolate its specific contribution.' The second sentence leaves the mathematical contribution unclear. The statement is from a fetch that was asked to quote verbatim; I did not check it against the PDF.
events.direction: Neutral for the bullet.
events.object: An explicit finite chain of non-aspherical presentation complexes, from a short balanced presentation of the binary icosahedral group (length two per a search summary), with zero maps on second homotopy and the identity property. It is not a counterexample to the Whitehead conjecture; the paper says the question is open.

events.what_happened: Laurent Bartholdi and Roman Mikhailov, 'Finite Chains of Two-Complexes and Acyclic Covers', arXiv:2610.10074 (submitted 7 Oct 2026; one version; licence CC BY 4.0; comment field 'Produced with help from AI'). Theorem A: for a two-complex K the following are equivalent: (1) for every n at least 1 there is a chain K = K0 proper-subset K1 proper-subset ... proper-subset Kn with every inclusion zero on pi_2; (2) K has a connected acyclic regular cover. If K is finite and acyclic the Ki can be chosen finite. Corollary B: the presentation complex of A = <x,y | x^2 y x^-1 y, x y^4 x y^-1> has, for every n, a chain of finite two-complexes K = K0 proper-subset ... proper-subset Kn with every inclusion zero on pi_2; the paper gives pi_2 of this complex as Z^119 (written 'Z119'). The paper says a negative answer to Whitehead's question would follow from an infinite such chain with a non-aspherical first term whose union is aspherical, and (per a fetch summary) that Theorem A 'does not produce an infinite chain'. The authors state that Theorem A 'has been formalized in Lean/Mathlib and will shortly be available on the Palomar repository'.
events.delivers: Finite chains only. Theorem A gives, for each finite length, chains of zero-on-pi_2 inclusions of two-complexes with a connected acyclic regular cover (finite if K is finite and acyclic). Corollary B gives such chains for the presentation complex of A, of every finite length. No infinite chain is produced, and no subcomplex of an aspherical complex is shown non-aspherical.
events.remains: The whole question. Per the authors and Howie's reduction, a negative answer needs an infinite chain (or a finite counterexample), and neither is produced.

machine_checked.system: Lean/Mathlib (claimed by the authors; not located)

events.directly_checkable: The presentation complex of A, its second homotopy group (the paper gives Z^119) and the zero inclusion maps can in principle be checked by computation from the presentation. I did not check them.
events.doubts: (1) The Lean/Mathlib formalisation is claimed but no repository was located; sorry status unknown. (2) Three days old; no reader engagement found. (3) The authors list AI tools as assisting 'with the proof of the main results' (see ai) without saying which steps they contributed. (4) Mikhailov's Aug 2026 paper and this paper both call the question open; neither cites Pasku or Kawauchi.
events.direction: Neutral for the conjecture as stated. It points to a possible route to a negative answer, but the finite chains it produces are not that route on its own.
events.object: The presentation complex K of A = <x,y | x^2 y x^-1 y, x y^4 x y^-1>, which the paper calls the presentation complex of SL(2,5): a finite, non-aspherical two-complex with, for every n, a chain of finite two-complexes K = K0 proper-subset ... proper-subset Kn whose inclusions are all zero on pi_2. The chains come from the existence statement of Theorem A; I did not check whether they are explicit. No Kn is claimed aspherical, and the paper says Theorem A does not give an infinite chain.

events.what_happened: OpenAI's openai/math repository lists 'A finitely generated counterexample to the Eilenberg-Ganea conjecture' (preprint folder and README dated 23 Sep 2026; 25 pages per a community index). The community index quotes the abstract as beginning 'We construct a finitely generated residually finite group of integral cohomological dimension two', and says it disproves the Eilenberg-Ganea conjecture. The repository and its 722-manuscript release were reported on 6 Oct 2026. Wikipedia's Whitehead and Eilenberg-Ganea pages report this as an OpenAI claim, citing the 23 Sep preprint. I could not read the PDF. I found no source that connects this entry to Whitehead's conjecture.
events.revisions: README date 23 Sep 2026; release on 6 Oct 2026 per secondary reports. The date of first public posting is not established; I have used 6 Oct, the date of the public release.
events.delivers: If correct, the Eilenberg-Ganea conjecture is false: a finitely generated residually finite group of integral cohomological dimension two without a two-dimensional Eilenberg-MacLane space (per the community index's abstract line). For Whitehead: nothing is stated. By Bestvina-Brady, Whitehead and Eilenberg-Ganea cannot both hold, so Eilenberg-Ganea failing does not decide Whitehead, and Whitehead being true would itself force Eilenberg-Ganea false.
events.remains: The whole Whitehead bullet, as far as this event shows.
events.doubts: (1) The PDF was not readable with my tools, so its method and any Whitehead remark are unverified. (2) The community index shows a Lean notes page for family 249, but no Lean mark on this paper's entry. A secondary write-up gives its evidence as 'source reporting and selected static proof-artifact inspection; no independent Lean execution'. OpenAI's README says some unformalized results 'could have issues'. (3) Wikipedia cites a 23 Sep date for a claim it dates to 6 Oct. (4) No expert engagement found yet.
events.direction: Against the Eilenberg-Ganea conjecture, if correct. No direction for Whitehead.
events.object: A finitely generated residually finite group of integral cohomological dimension 2, claimed to have no two-dimensional Eilenberg-MacLane space (community index's quote of the abstract). The construction and whether it is explicit were not read.

disputes.summary: Kawauchi's 2023 arXiv paper says E. Pasku's preprint (arXiv:2107.12293, first posted July 2021) reports the same result by a purely group-theoretic argument, and calls Kawauchi's own argument 'much different'. Pasku's claim predates Kawauchi's. Neither paper engages with the other's proof, as far as I can see.

ProofAtlas's individual Whitehead page (checked 7 Aug 2026) says no proof or counterexample is known and lists the Pasku and Kawauchi claims as under review. A search summary reported that ProofAtlas's open-problems list shows the conjecture as 'source-reported proved' on the strength of the OpenAI release of 6 Oct 2026. I could not find such an entry: the open-problems page I read covers ranks 1 to about 163 and the whole text except its last roughly 8,000 characters, and it has no Whitehead entry. The search summary's claim is not supported by anything I could open.

Wikipedia's Whitehead and Eilenberg-Ganea pages report an OpenAI claimed counterexample to the Eilenberg-Ganea conjecture, dated 6 Oct 2026, citing a preprint dated 23 Sep 2026. Neither page says the claim bears on Whitehead's conjecture. Only the Eilenberg-Ganea claim is reported on them, and the date of first public posting is not established.
Kawauchi's author website lists the 2023 paper as published in J. Math. Techniques Comput. Math. 3(5) (2024). The arXiv record carries no journal reference, and I could not find the journal record.

summary: No event in the window (since 26 January 2024) establishes or refutes the Whitehead conjecture in any source I could open. Two single-author arXiv papers claim the full statement. Pasku (arXiv:2107.12293, first posted 26 July 2021, revised 5 Oct 2026) proves that deleting any one relator from an aspherical presentation of the trivial group leaves an aspherical presentation; with Ivanov's 1999 reduction this would settle the question. Kawauchi (arXiv:2303.04368, first posted 8 March 2023, revised 9 April 2024) claims the full statement by a ribbon sphere-link argument, which his website lists as published in a journal I could not find. Neither has a referee report, correction, or citation by a topologist that I could find, and the two most recent papers by Roman Mikhailov (arXiv:2608.20270, 20 Aug 2026; and arXiv:2610.10074 with Laurent Bartholdi, 7 Oct 2026) say the question remains open and cite neither. Mikhailov is an author of the second, so the two are not independent. The 7 Oct paper is the only AI-credited mathematics on the bullet that I found. Its authors say ChatGPT 6 Astra, Claude 5.5 Fable and Aristotle 'were used to assist with the proof of the main results', and it constructs finite chains of zero-on-pi_2 inclusions (Theorem A, Corollary B). The authors themselves say a negative answer would need an infinite chain, and the paper does not produce one. Its Lean/Mathlib formalisation of Theorem A is claimed but not located. Restricted results in the window include Harlander and Rosebrock (arXiv:2511.15212, Nov 2025) on local indicability for LOT-type complexes. Earlier reductions and partial results are recorded as events: Howie (1983), Ivanov (1999), Cerdeiro and Minian (2012), Kawauchi (Dec 2022, contractible finite 2-complexes), Harlander and Rosebrock (Dec 2012, injective LOTs) and Mikhovich (2021, rational and p-adic analogues only). The OpenAI release of 6 Oct 2026 includes a claimed counterexample to the Eilenberg-Ganea conjecture (family 249). By Bestvina-Brady it does not decide Whitehead: the two cannot both hold, so Eilenberg-Ganea failing says nothing about Whitehead, while Whitehead true would force Eilenberg-Ganea false. I could not read that preprint, so its method and any remark on Whitehead are unverified. I found no source that credits AI with the Whitehead mathematics, and no AI-attributed Whitehead proof or counterexample. Close calls: (1) whether the 2021 Pasku and 2023 Kawauchi claims count in the window. Both first arguments predate 26 January 2024, and only their 2026 revisions fall inside it. (2) Whether the Bartholdi-Mikhailov finite chains move the bullet. On the authors' own account they do not. (3) Whether 'assist with the proof of the main results' is load-bearing: the authors do not say which steps the AI tools contributed to. Dates: the Bartholdi-Mikhailov date is the arXiv submission date (7 Oct 2026); one search summary gave 3 Oct, which I did not use. Ivanov's and Howie's full texts were not opened; their statements are from abstracts and secondary sources.
competing_reading: If Pasku's argument is correct, the question has been settled since 2021 and the window holds only the revision of 5 Oct 2026. Under that reading, the 'open' statements from 2026 are field judgements that would have noticed a verified proof, so the lack of engagement is a sign the argument is not believed rather than that nobody looked. Alternatively, the silence could be sociological: arXiv preprints by unknown authors on a famous problem are often ignored for years, and the cited papers by Mikhailov merely reflect what he knew. On either reading, the Bartholdi-Mikhailov AI credit could be read as load-bearing, since 'assist with the proof of the main results' is the authors' own wording. Read the other way, it is writing and checking assistance, since the same sentence also names 'the redaction of the manuscript'.
what_would_settle_it: (1) A published review or referee report of Pasku (arXiv:2107.12293) or Kawauchi (arXiv:2303.04368), for example a MathSciNet or zbMATH review, or a journal record for Kawauchi's claimed 2024 publication. (2) A specialist note that finds or closes a gap in the key steps: Pasku's Section 3 weak-dominion equivalence and Section 4 exactness argument, or Kawauchi's Lemma 3.1 base change, Lemma 4.1 and Lemma 5.1. (3) A Lean formalisation of either reduction, sorry-free, or the Palomar repository for Bartholdi and Mikhailov's Theorem A, with its sorry status. (4) The text of OpenAI's Eilenberg-Ganea preprint and any statement in it about Whitehead's conjecture, together with the Lean status of family 249. (5) A later paper that cites Pasku or Kawauchi and states the status of the Whitehead question explicitly.

judgement.why: Only two events claim the whole statement, Pasku (July 2021) and Kawauchi (March 2023). Both first appeared before the snapshot, and the record shows no new mathematics in their later revisions (Oct 2026 and Apr 2024), so both are dated before it. Both are unreviewed and doubtful: nobody has taken them up, and the 2026 specialist papers call the question open without citing either. They are not knocked down, because no specific unanswered error is on the record. After the snapshot, nothing settles a case or moves the statement. Harlander-Rosebrock 2025 concerns local indicability; DR subcomplexes of DR complexes are DR trivially, and injective LOTs were already known to be aspherical, so it adds no case of asphericity. Mikhailov's finite chain answers Hitchman's question. Bartholdi-Mikhailov produce finite chains that the authors themselves say do not give the infinite chain a counterexample needs, so the scope is none. Their AI statement says the tools assisted 'with the proof of the main results', so that event is marked assisted. The OpenAI release is about Eilenberg-Ganea, a different conjecture; by Bestvina-Brady its failure does not decide Whitehead, so it is a variant. Its AI role is taken from the README's statement about the release as a whole.
judgement.doubts: Whether Pasku 2021 should be not_credible rather than doubtful is a close call. Several F10 signals are present, but the author works in the area with a serious method. The choice cannot change the outcome, because the event predates the snapshot and is unreviewed. The OpenAI AI credit rests on a release-wide README sentence, not on a statement specific to this paper. The Bartholdi-Mikhailov quote does not say which steps the AI contributed.
